title: Backups and recovery
summary: Daily backups vs point-in-time recovery, the two numbers to agree with a client, how to restore without making things worse, and why an untested backup is only a hope.
youWillLearn: The difference between a daily backup and point-in-time recovery
RPO and RTO: how much data and how much time you can afford to lose
How to bring back deleted rows without wiping out newer ones
What database backups do not cover, and why you must test a restore

glossary.backup: A saved copy of your data from a moment in time, kept somewhere else, so you can bring it back after a mistake.
glossary.snapshot: A full copy of the database taken at one moment, for example every night at 03:00.
glossary.point-in-time recovery: Restoring the database to any exact second in the past, not only to the last nightly copy.
glossary.WAL: Write-ahead log: Postgres's running diary of every change, written before the change is applied.
glossary.RPO: Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
glossary.RTO: Recovery time objective: how long the app can afford to be down while you restore.
glossary.replica: A live copy of a database that follows every change of the original within seconds.
glossary.restore drill: A planned practice run where you restore a backup into a spare database and check the data is really there.
glossary.pg_dump: The standard Postgres tool that exports a database into a file you can store anywhere and load back later.

steps.title: Where Notely keeps its notes
body: Notely's 5,000 users reach the app server, the computer running Notely's code. It keeps their 200,000 notes in the database: Postgres, run for us by Supabase.
Maya also works with Claude Code, the AI assistant that writes code on her laptop. It can run commands on that same database when she asks.

scene.caption: Users reach the database through the app server. Claude Code can reach it too.

steps.title: One query, every note gone
body: Tuesday, 14:05. Maya asks Claude Code to clean up test notes. It runs a delete on the live database, but the filter has a bug. Every note in Notely is gone.
A database has no undo button. The only way back is a copy made before 14:05. Does she have one, and from when?

code.code:
-- meant: delete notes of the test account
delete from notes
where user_id = user_id; -- always true: every row
code.caption: Comparing a column with itself matches every row. One wrong word, the whole table.

changes: ~ Claude Code → Database: a delete that matches every row
~ Notes in DB 200,000 → 0
~ Work lost None → All notes

scene.caption: One buggy delete empties the notes table.

steps.title: Backups are copies in time
body: A backup is a copy of the data from a past moment, stored away from the live database. Restoring means going back to that moment.
The question is always which moments you can go back to. That decides how much work is lost. Here is Notely's timeline: nightly copies, the last good second, then the bad query.

callout.text: Figma's version history. Autosaves let you go back to any recent moment. Named versions are fewer, but survive longer. A database has both kinds too.

changes: − 5,000 users, App Server, Claude Code, Database: we look at time
+ Mon 03:00, Tue 03:00: nightly copies
+ Tue 14:04, Tue 14:05: last good moment, then the bad query

scene.caption: A timeline from left to right. Which moments can Notely go back to?

steps.title: Nightly snapshots lose the day
body: The basic kind is a nightly snapshot: a full copy of the database, once a day, kept for some days.
Restoring Tuesday 03:00 brings the notes back. But everything written between 03:00 and 14:05 is gone: eleven hours of notes, sign-ups and summaries. For a notes app, that is a lot of angry users.

callout.text: Check your plan before you need it. Supabase's paid plans include daily backups, and point-in-time recovery is an add-on. On a free plan, do not count on any backup existing.

changes: ~ Tue 03:00: the copy a nightly backup restores
~ Tue 14:04: out of reach, eleven hours later
~ Work lost All notes → 11 hours

scene.caption: A nightly snapshot only reaches back to 03:00.

steps.title: Point-in-time: rewind to the second
body: Postgres writes every change to a running diary first: the WAL. Keep the nightly snapshot plus the diary since then, and you can replay changes up to any exact moment.
That is point-in-time recovery. Maya picks 14:04:59: the snapshot is loaded, then every change is replayed until one second before the bad query.
changes: + WAL: Postgres's diary of every change since 03:00
~ Tue 14:04: reachable again, by replaying the diary
~ Work lost 11 hours → 1 second

scene.caption: Snapshot plus diary: replay every change up to 14:04:59.

steps.title: Two numbers to agree with a client
body: Before choosing a backup setup, ask two questions. How much recent data can we lose? That is the RPO. How long can the app be down while we restore? That is the RTO.
Nightly snapshots give an RPO of up to a day. Point-in-time gets it down to seconds, and costs more.

callout.text: Building for a client, like a salon's booking app? Ask: "If we lost today's bookings, how bad is that?" No-shows and angry customers justify paying for point-in-time recovery. Agree it in writing.

changes: ~ Tue 03:00: nightly copies, RPO up to a day
~ WAL: point-in-time, RPO of seconds
~ Tue 14:04 and Tue 14:05 step back

scene.caption: Two setups, two very different amounts of lost work.

steps.title: Restore beside, then copy back
body: Restoring over the live database would also erase everything since 14:05: new sign-ups, new notes. If your provider allows it, restore into a separate database instead.
Then copy back only what was lost. Export the restored notes table, load it next to the live one as restored_notes, and insert the missing rows.

code.caption: Rows that still exist are skipped, so nothing written after 14:05 is overwritten.

changes: + Restored DB: a separate copy as of 14:04:59
+ Database: the live one, back in view
~ Notes in DB 0 → 200,000

scene.caption: Only the missing rows travel from the restored copy into the live database.

steps.title: What the database backup misses
body: Database backups cover database rows. Files users upload are not inside them; the database only holds their names. Neither are your settings or keys.
A replica, a live copy that follows every change, is not a backup either: it copies the delete within seconds. Keep one extra copy outside your provider too, made with pg_dump.

code.caption: Run it on a schedule (a GitHub Action works) and store the file encrypted, somewhere else.

changes: − Restored DB
+ Replica: a live copy, so it copies the delete too
+ Files: uploads, not inside database backups
+ Extra Copy: a pg_dump file kept somewhere else

scene.caption: A replica copies mistakes, files sit outside the backup, and an extra copy lives elsewhere.

steps.title: An untested backup is a hope
body: Backups fail quietly: a job that stopped months ago, a dump with no data, a password nobody remembers. You find out on the worst day.
Run a restore drill every few months. Restore into a spare database, count the rows, open a few notes, and time it. That time is your real RTO. Write the steps down.

callout.text: Before Claude Code runs any delete, update or migration on production, ask: is there a backup from the last hour? Run a select count(*) with the same where first. Wrap it in begin;, check the count, then commit; or rollback;.

changes: − Replica, Files
+ Scratch DB: a spare database for practice restores
~ Database steps back

scene.caption: The extra copy is restored into a spare database, counted and timed.

steps.title: Recap: copies you have actually tried
body: Nightly snapshots lose up to a day. Point-in-time recovery replays the WAL to the second before the mistake. Agree on RPO and RTO with the client and pick the setup to match.
Restore beside production and copy back. Files and replicas are not backups. Practice the restore before you need it.
changes: ~ Database back in focus, with a tested copy beside it

scene.caption: A live database, an extra copy, and proof that the copy restores.

quiz.question: Notely only has nightly backups at 03:00. A bad query deletes notes at 17:00. What does a restore give back?

options.why: That would need point-in-time recovery. A nightly snapshot only knows the database as it was at 03:00.

options.text: The data as of 03:00. Everything written after that is lost.
options.why: A snapshot is one moment. Fourteen hours of new notes are not in it, which is why the RPO of nightly backups is up to a day.
Restoring a backup is exactly how you undo a delete. The question is only how recent the copy is.

quiz.question: A client says: "We have a read replica, so we are covered for backups." What do you tell them?

options.text: Correct, a replica is a full copy of the data.
options.why: It is a copy, but a live one. It follows the original within seconds, mistakes included.

options.text: A replica is only useful for analytics.
options.why: Replicas help with read load and failover, as you saw in system design. They do not protect against bad writes.

options.text: A replica copies a bad delete within seconds. You still need backups.
options.why: Replicas protect against a server dying, not against a wrong query. Backups let you go back in time; replicas cannot.

quiz.question: Claude Code proposes delete from bookings where status = 'test'; on a client's production database. What do you do first?

options.text: Run select count(*) from bookings where status = 'test'; and confirm a recent backup exists.
options.why: The count shows exactly how many rows the delete will hit, before anything changes. A fresh backup means a mistake is recoverable.

options.text: Run it. The where clause makes it safe.
options.why: The query in this lesson also had a where clause. A filter can still match far more rows than you expect.

options.text: Run it on production, then check the app.
options.why: Checking after a destructive query only tells you how bad the damage is.

takeaways: Nightly snapshots can lose up to a day. Point-in-time recovery rewinds to the second.
Agree on RPO (data you can lose) and RTO (time you can be down) with the client, in writing.
Restore into a separate database, then copy back only the missing rows.
Database backups skip uploaded files and settings, and a replica is not a backup.
Run a restore drill. A backup you have never restored is only a hope.
